summary: Extends IS-IS to carry administrative tags in link state data, so operators can control and manage IP prefix distribution through policy. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets network owners stick labels on routes and make rules by label, such as handing out all red-labeled ones here.

questions: what is an is-is administrative tag
how do is-is route tags work
how to leak prefixes between is-is levels
subtitle: Attach numeric labels to IP prefixes in IS-IS so routers can apply policy by tag instead of by prefix.

tldr.problem: Operators of multi-level IS-IS networks need an easy way to control which IP prefixes are distributed where, but a router has no way to tell prefixes with one property from those with another.
tldr.mechanism: Two new sub-TLVs, with type codes 1 and 2, carry one or more 32-bit or 64-bit administrative tags on an IP prefix, and the tag travels with the prefix as it is flooded.
tldr.outcome: Routers can match on a tag in policy, for example to leak tagged prefixes between levels, while the meaning of any tag is left to the operator.

today: RFC 5130 is a Proposed Standard and its metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it, so it remains the definition of the IS-IS administrative tag sub-TLVs.

sections.title: Why Prefixes Need Tags
sections.content:
IS-IS distributes IPv4 prefix reachability as defined in RFC 1195 and extended in RFC 3784, and IPv6 reachability through later extensions. The extended IP Reachability TLV (TLV 135) already supports a larger metric space, an up/down bit that marks redistribution between levels, an IP prefix, and sub-TLVs for extra information about the prefix. TLV 235 adds Multi-Topology membership (RFC 5120). The IPv6 prefix information is in TLV 236 and TLV 237.

This document adds two Administrative Tag sub-TLVs to TLV 135, 235, 236 and 237, to carry administrative information about an IP prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Routes already carry some information, like how far away they are. This adds a spot for a sticky note that the network owner can write on.

sections.title: The Two Tag Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The tags are unsigned integers associated with an IP prefix. The 32-bit form is sub-TLV 1: one octet of type (value 1), one octet of length (a multiple of 4), then one or more 4-octet tags. The 64-bit form is sub-TLV 2: type value 2, a length that is a multiple of 8, then one or more 8-octet tags.

Example uses given by the RFC are carrying BGP standard or extended communities and controlling redistribution between levels and areas, between routing protocols, or between multiple instances of IS-IS on one router. How tags are used is beyond the scope of the document and left to the implementer or operator.

On receipt, an implementation MAY consider only one tag, in which case it MUST use the first and ignore the rest. A tag value of zero is reserved and SHOULD be treated as "no tag".
sections.plainLanguage: A tag is just a number on a route. You can use a short number or a long one, and a route can carry several. A zero means no label at all.

sections.title: Tag Order and Propagation
sections.content:
The order of tags has no implied meaning. Each tag SHOULD be treated as an independent identifier that policy MAY act on, and swapping tag A and tag B SHOULD NOT change the meaning of the set. There is one exception for propagation: when TLVs with several tags move between levels, an implementation SHOULD keep the first tag first, so that routers recognizing only a single tag see the same thing at every level.

Any IS that receives an LSP with these TLVs and sub-TLVs MAY act on the tag values. If it must change them, for example at an area boundary, the TLVs SHOULD be copied into the newly generated Level-1 or Level-2 LSP, and the content MAY change as the policy dictates. If nothing changes, the sub-TLVs SHOULD be copied in order.
sections.plainLanguage: Tags are a bag of labels, not a list in rank order. But if you pass the bag along, keep the label that old routers read first in the first spot.

sections.title: What a Compliant Router Must Do
sections.content:
A compliant implementation MUST be able to assign one tag to an IP prefix in TLV 135, 235, 236 and 237. It MUST be able to interpret a single tag, or the first tag when there are several.

It MAY assign more than one tag, MAY interpret the second and later tags, and MAY rewrite or remove tags when propagating TLVs between levels.

Implementations that support one tag and those that support many can coexist in a domain. An implementation using multiple tags SHOULD therefore put any tag that every system must interpret first.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router has to understand at least one label per route. Understanding more is a bonus, so put the label everybody must read first.

sections.title: Leaking Prefixes by Tag
sections.content:
An administrator ties a tag value to some interesting property. When IS-IS advertises a prefix with that property, it adds the tag to that prefix's IP reachability TLV, and the tag "sticks" to the prefix as it is flooded through the domain.

In the RFC's example, the goal is to leak Level-1 prefixes with property A from Level 2 to the Level-1 router R1. Tag 100 is associated with property A, and R5 attaches it to the TLV for prefix 1.1.2.0/24. Router R2 has a policy to match prefixes with tag 100 and leak them to Level 1.

The RFC admits that matching the single prefix would be as easy here. The mechanism pays off when many routers must apply a policy to a large number of prefixes sharing a property.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of listing every red house by address, you paint a red dot on each one. Then a rule such as "send all red-dot houses this way" is easy to write.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The document says it raises no new security issues for IS-IS, because annotations on IP prefixes should not pass outside the administrative control of the network operator of the IS-IS domain. Allowing that would violate the spirit of Interior Gateway Protocols in general and IS-IS in particular.

IANA assigned type code 1 to the 32-bit Administrative Tag sub-TLV and type code 2 to the 64-bit one. The manageability section states that these extensions have been designed, developed and deployed for many years and have no new impact on management and operation of IS-IS through this standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: The labels are meant to stay inside your own network, like notes on your own fridge, so they add no new risk.

root.label: R2
root.note: Policy: match tag 100, leak to L1
